title: Healing from Trauma: Reclaiming Your Life After PTSD
summary: A compassionate, evidence-based CBT program designed to help you heal from trauma and reclaim your life. Through trauma-informed approaches, cognitive processing, and gradual exposure techniques, you'll learn to process traumatic memories, challenge unhelpful beliefs, and rebuild a sense of safety, meaning, and connection.

modules.title: Module 1 • Understanding Trauma: The Foundation of Healing
modules.overview: Trauma is not what happens to you—it's what happens inside you as a result of what happened. This module helps you understand trauma, how it affects the brain and body, and why your responses make sense given what you've experienced. We explore Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) and its symptoms: re-experiencing (flashbacks, nightmares), avoidance, negative changes in thoughts and mood, and hyperarousal. Understanding these symptoms helps you see that your responses are normal reactions to abnormal events. The module explains how trauma affects the brain—particularly the amygdala, hippocampus, and prefrontal cortex—and why this leads to symptoms like hypervigilance, memory fragmentation, and difficulty regulating emotions. You'll learn about the window of tolerance—the optimal zone of arousal where you can process information and regulate emotions. Trauma narrows this window, making it easier to become overwhelmed or shut down. Self-monitoring begins here. You'll start tracking your symptoms, triggers, and responses in a safe, structured way. This awareness is the foundation for healing. Finally, we emphasize safety and self-compassion. Healing from trauma is possible, but it requires patience, support, and self-kindness. This program provides tools; your courage provides the healing.
takeaways: Trauma responses are normal reactions to abnormal events—not signs of weakness.
Understanding how trauma affects the brain helps explain your symptoms.
Safety and stabilization are the foundation of trauma recovery.
Self-compassion is essential—healing takes time and patience.
exercises: Safety Assessment: Identify what helps you feel safe right now. This might include: People, Places, Activities, Objects, Practices. Create a list you can refer to when you need support.

Symptom Tracking: For one week, track your PTSD symptoms. Note: Which symptoms appear, When they occur, What triggers them, How intense they are (1-10), What helps. Track without judgment—just observe.
Window of Tolerance Check-In: Three times per day, check in with yourself: 'Where am I right now? Am I in my window of tolerance, hyperaroused, or hypoaroused? What do I need?'
Self-Compassion Practice: When you notice difficult symptoms or responses, practice self-compassion: 'This is a normal response to trauma. I'm doing my best. Healing takes time.'
homework: Complete your Safety Assessment. Keep this list accessible. Add to it as you discover new sources of safety.
Maintain your Symptom Tracking for one week. Review patterns without judgment. Notice what triggers symptoms and what helps.
Practice Window of Tolerance Check-Ins daily. Notice patterns in when you're in or out of your window.
Write a compassionate letter to yourself about your trauma experience. Acknowledge how difficult it's been, validate your responses, and remind yourself that healing is possible.

modules.title: Module 2 • Safety and Stabilization: Building Your Foundation
modules.overview: Safety is the foundation of trauma recovery. Before you can process traumatic memories, you need to feel safe in your body and in your environment. This module focuses on building safety and stabilization skills. We explore grounding techniques—practical tools for staying present when you feel overwhelmed or disconnected. These techniques help you return to the present moment when trauma responses pull you into the past. The module introduces emotional regulation skills—ways to manage intense emotions without becoming overwhelmed or shutting down. These skills widen your window of tolerance. You'll learn about creating physical safety—making your environment feel safe and secure. This might include changes to your living space, routines, or boundaries with others. We explore the importance of social support and healthy boundaries. Trauma can make it hard to trust others, but connection is essential for healing. You'll learn to identify safe people and set boundaries that protect you. Finally, we introduce self-care practices that support your nervous system. Trauma takes a toll on your body. Taking care of yourself physically, emotionally, and spiritually is essential for recovery.
takeaways: Safety and stabilization must come before trauma processing.
Grounding techniques help you stay present when trauma responses pull you into the past.
Emotional regulation skills widen your window of tolerance.
Healthy boundaries protect you while allowing connection.
exercises: Grounding Techniques Practice: Practice each grounding technique daily for one week. Notice which ones work best for you. Create a personal grounding toolkit.
Emotional Check-In: Three times per day, check in with your emotions: 'What am I feeling? Where do I feel it in my body? What do I need?' Practice naming and tolerating emotions.
Safety Space Creation: Create a physical safe space in your home. This might be a corner, a room, or even a chair. Make it comfortable, calming, and yours. Spend time there daily.
Boundary Practice: Identify one boundary you need to set. Practice setting it clearly and kindly. Notice how it feels to protect yourself.
Support System Map: Identify people in your life. Categorize them: Safe and supportive, Unsafe or unsupportive, Neutral. Focus on building relationships with safe people.
homework: Practice grounding techniques daily. Use them whenever you feel overwhelmed or disconnected. Notice which techniques work best for you.
Complete your Safety Space. Spend at least 10 minutes there daily, practicing grounding or simply being present.
Practice emotional check-ins three times per day. Build your capacity to recognize, name, and tolerate emotions.
Set one boundary this week. Practice protecting yourself while staying connected to safe people.

modules.title: Module 3 • Understanding Trauma's Impact: Beliefs and Meaning
modules.overview: Trauma doesn't just affect your memories—it affects your beliefs about yourself, others, and the world. These beliefs, called 'stuck points,' can keep you trapped in trauma responses long after the event is over. We explore common stuck points in trauma: safety ('The world is dangerous'), trust ('I can't trust anyone'), power ('I'm powerless'), esteem ('I'm damaged/broken'), and intimacy ('I don't deserve love'). The module helps you identify your own stuck points—beliefs that developed as a result of trauma and that now interfere with your life. These beliefs feel true, but they're interpretations, not facts. You'll learn to recognize how stuck points affect your thoughts, feelings, and behaviors. Understanding this connection helps you see how changing beliefs can change your life. We introduce the concept of 'assimilation' and 'accommodation'—how trauma can lead you to either blame yourself (assimilation) or see the world as entirely dangerous (accommodation). Recovery involves finding balance. Finally, we begin the process of challenging stuck points, gently and compassionately. You'll learn that beliefs can change, that you can develop new, more balanced perspectives that honor your experience while allowing you to move forward.
takeaways: Trauma affects your beliefs about yourself, others, and the world.
Stuck points are beliefs that developed from trauma and now interfere with your life.
Understanding how beliefs affect thoughts, feelings, and behaviors is key to change.
Beliefs can be challenged and changed—they're interpretations, not facts.
exercises: Stuck Point Identification: Identify stuck points in each of the five areas (safety, trust, power, esteem, intimacy). Write them down. Notice how they feel true, but also notice how they might be too extreme.
Belief Impact Exercise: Choose one stuck point. Explore how it affects your: Thoughts, Feelings, Behaviors. Notice the connection between belief and experience.
Assimilation/Accommodation Check: For each stuck point, ask: 'Is this assimilation (blaming myself) or accommodation (seeing everything as dangerous)?' Notice patterns.
Balanced Belief Development: For each stuck point, try to develop a more balanced belief. Example: 'The world can be dangerous AND safe' instead of 'The world is entirely dangerous.'
homework: Complete your Stuck Point Identification. Review your stuck points weekly, noticing how they affect your life.
Choose one stuck point to work with. Explore how it affects your thoughts, feelings, and behaviors. Practice developing a more balanced belief.
Practice balanced thinking daily. When you notice extreme beliefs, try to find a more balanced perspective that honors your experience while allowing movement forward.

modules.title: Module 4 • Processing Trauma: Writing and Exposure
modules.overview: Processing trauma involves gradually and safely confronting traumatic memories. This module introduces writing and exposure techniques that help you process what happened in a controlled, supportive way. We explore the importance of timing—processing should only happen when you have adequate safety and stabilization skills. Rushing into processing can be retraumatizing. The module introduces trauma narratives—writing about your trauma experience in detail. This helps integrate fragmented memories and process emotions. You'll learn to write your narrative gradually, at your own pace. You'll learn about gradual exposure—systematically facing trauma reminders in a controlled way. This helps your brain learn that reminders are not the same as the trauma itself. We explore how to manage intense emotions during processing. Processing trauma can be difficult. You'll learn techniques to stay within your window of tolerance while processing. Finally, we emphasize self-care and support during processing. Processing trauma is hard work. Taking care of yourself and having support is essential.
takeaways: Trauma processing should only happen when you have adequate safety and stabilization skills.
Writing trauma narratives helps integrate fragmented memories.
Gradual exposure helps your brain learn that reminders are not the trauma itself.
Self-care and support are essential during trauma processing.
exercises: Readiness Assessment: Assess your readiness for trauma processing. Do you have: Adequate safety and stabilization skills? Support system? Ability to manage intense emotions? If not, focus on Module 2 first.
Trauma Narrative Outline: Create an outline of your trauma narrative. Include: Facts, Sensory details, Thoughts and feelings, Aftermath, Meaning. Don't write the full narrative yet—just outline it.
Exposure Hierarchy: Create a list of trauma reminders, ranked from least to most anxiety-provoking. Start with the easiest items.

Emotion Management Plan: Create a plan for managing intense emotions during processing. Include: Grounding techniques, Emotional regulation skills, Self-compassion practices, Support people, When to take breaks.
homework: Complete your Readiness Assessment. If you're not ready for processing, focus on safety and stabilization (Module 2) first.
Create your Trauma Narrative Outline. Take your time. There's no rush.
Begin writing your trauma narrative gradually. Start with facts. Add details slowly. Take breaks when needed. Use grounding techniques if you become overwhelmed.
Practice exposure with the easiest items on your hierarchy. Face them repeatedly until anxiety decreases. Move to the next item only when ready.

modules.title: Module 5 • Cognitive Restructuring: Challenging Stuck Points
modules.overview: Cognitive restructuring helps you challenge and change stuck points—beliefs that developed from trauma and now interfere with your life. This module teaches you to examine these beliefs, gather evidence, and develop more balanced perspectives. We explore the Thought Record—a structured tool for examining stuck points. You'll learn to identify stuck points, examine evidence for and against them, and develop balanced alternatives. The module helps you challenge common stuck points: self-blame ('It was my fault'), safety ('The world is entirely dangerous'), trust ('I can't trust anyone'), power ('I'm powerless'), and esteem ('I'm damaged'). You'll learn to distinguish between facts and interpretations. Stuck points often feel like facts, but they're interpretations. Learning to see this distinction is key to change. We explore the concept of 'stuck point logs'—tracking stuck points as they appear and systematically challenging them. This helps you develop new, more balanced beliefs. Finally, we introduce behavioral experiments—testing new beliefs in real life. These experiments provide evidence that challenges old stuck points and supports new beliefs.
takeaways: Stuck points are interpretations, not facts—they can be challenged and changed.
Thought records help you examine stuck points systematically.
Distinguishing between facts and interpretations is key to change.
Behavioral experiments provide real-world evidence for new beliefs.
exercises: Stuck Point Log: Keep a log of stuck points as they appear. For each, complete a thought record: Identify the stuck point, Notice when it appears, Examine evidence for and against, Develop a balanced belief, Notice how this affects your feelings and behaviors.
Common Stuck Point Challenge: Choose one common stuck point (self-blame, safety, trust, power, or esteem). Complete a detailed thought record. Challenge it systematically. Develop a balanced belief.
Facts vs. Interpretations Exercise: For a recent situation, identify: Facts—what actually happened, Interpretations—what meanings you assigned. Practice distinguishing between them.

Behavioral Experiment: Choose one stuck point. Design an experiment to test a new, balanced belief. For example, if your stuck point is 'I can't trust anyone,' experiment with trusting a safe person in a small way. Document results.
homework: Maintain your Stuck Point Log for two weeks. Complete thought records for stuck points as they appear. Notice patterns.
Choose one major stuck point to work with. Complete a detailed thought record. Challenge it systematically. Develop and practice a balanced belief.
Practice distinguishing facts from interpretations daily. When you notice interpretations, ask: 'Is this a fact or an interpretation? What's the evidence?'
Conduct at least one behavioral experiment per week. Test new beliefs in real life. Document results and notice what you learn.

modules.title: Module 6 • Reclaiming Your Life: Behavioral Activation and Values
modules.overview: Trauma can make you withdraw from life. This module helps you reclaim your life by re-engaging with activities, relationships, and values that matter to you. We explore behavioral activation—gradually re-engaging with activities you've been avoiding. This helps break the cycle of avoidance that maintains PTSD. The module introduces values clarification—identifying what matters to you, what gives your life meaning. Trauma can make you lose sight of your values. Reconnecting with them helps you rebuild meaning. You'll learn to create an activity hierarchy—a list of activities ranked by how important they are to you and how much anxiety they cause. This helps you prioritize and gradually re-engage. We explore the importance of relationships in recovery. Trauma can make you isolate. Reconnecting with safe people is essential for healing. Finally, we introduce the concept of 'post-traumatic growth'—the possibility of growing from trauma, finding meaning, and living a rich, full life despite what happened.
takeaways: Behavioral activation helps break the cycle of avoidance.
Reconnecting with values helps rebuild meaning.
Gradual re-engagement with activities and relationships supports recovery.
Post-traumatic growth is possible—you can grow from trauma.
exercises: Values Identification: Identify your top 5-10 values. Write about why each matters to you. How have you lived these values in the past? How can you live them now?
Activity Hierarchy: List activities you've been avoiding. Rank them by importance and anxiety. Start with high-importance, low-anxiety activities.
Behavioral Activation Plan: Choose 3-5 activities from your hierarchy. Schedule them for this week. Commit to doing them, even if you don't feel like it.
Relationship Reconnection: Identify 2-3 safe people you want to reconnect with. Make a plan to reach out. Start small—a text, a call, a brief meet-up.
Post-Traumatic Growth Reflection: Reflect on areas where you might be growing: Appreciation for life, Relationships, Personal strength, New possibilities, Spiritual growth. Write about this.
homework: Complete your Values Identification. Review your values weekly. Ask: 'How am I living my values? What can I do to align more with them?'
Create your Activity Hierarchy. Start re-engaging with high-importance, low-anxiety activities. Gradually work your way up.
Schedule and complete behavioral activation activities weekly. Notice how re-engagement affects your mood, connection, and sense of self.
Reach out to at least one safe person this week. Start rebuilding connections. Notice how it feels.
Reflect on post-traumatic growth monthly. Notice areas where you're growing, even if growth is small.

modules.title: Module 7 • Integration and Moving Forward: Your Path Ahead
modules.overview: The final module consolidates your learning and helps you create a plan for continued healing. Recovery from trauma is a journey, not a destination. This module prepares you for that journey. We review your progress—acknowledging how far you've come, the skills you've learned, the growth you've experienced. Celebrating progress is important. The module helps you create a maintenance plan—strategies for maintaining your progress and preventing relapse. This includes: Daily practices, Weekly practices, Warning signs, Action plans, Supports. We explore how to handle setbacks. Setbacks are normal—they don't mean you've failed. Learning to navigate setbacks without derailing your progress is crucial. You'll learn about continuing your healing journey—how to keep growing, processing, and reclaiming your life. Healing doesn't end when the program ends. Finally, we celebrate your courage and set intentions for continued growth. You've done hard work. You've shown incredible courage. You've reclaimed your life. This is worth celebrating.
takeaways: Recovery from trauma is a journey, not a destination.
A maintenance plan helps you stay on track and prevent relapse.
Setbacks are normal—they don't mean you've failed.
Continuing your healing journey supports long-term recovery.
exercises: Progress Reflection: Write about your progress. What have you learned? What tools work best for you? What challenges have you overcome? What are you proud of?
Maintenance Plan Creation: Create your personal maintenance plan. Include: Daily practices, Weekly practices, Warning signs, Action plan, Supports, Values. Make it specific and actionable.
Setback Response Plan: Create a plan for responding to setbacks. Include: How you'll recognize setbacks, What tools you'll use, Who you'll reach out to, How you'll practice self-compassion.
Continuing Journey Map: Map out how you'll continue your healing journey. What will you focus on? What goals do you have? What supports will you use?

Celebration Ritual: Plan a celebration ritual to acknowledge your progress. This might include: Reflecting on your journey, Acknowledging your courage, Setting intentions for continued growth, Doing something meaningful to mark this milestone.
homework: Complete your Progress Reflection. Review it regularly. Celebrate your growth.
Finalize your Maintenance Plan. Share it with a trusted person. Review it weekly and adjust as needed.
Create your Setback Response Plan. Practice it when setbacks occur. Notice how it helps.
Map your Continuing Journey. Set goals. Make plans. Keep moving forward.
Complete your Celebration Ritual. Acknowledge your courage. Celebrate your progress. Set intentions for continued growth.

aiSupport.systemPrompt: Help the user apply one concrete module step at a time. Do not diagnose. Escalate urgent safety concerns to emergency care.
